question: रैट-होल खनन ककस राज्य से सिंबिंर्ित है?
explanation:  The term “rat hole" refers to the narrow pits dug into the ground, typically just large enough for one person to descend and extract coal.  The coal is manually extracted using primitive tools such as pickaxes, shovels, and baskets.  It is a method of manual drilling most common in Meghalaya, especially in the West Jaintia Hills, East Jaintia Hills, and West Khasi Hills.  Rat-hole mining is broadly classified into two categories: Side-cutting procedure and box-cutting.  In the side-cutting procedure, narrow tunnels are dug on the hill slopes, and workers go inside until they find the coal seam.  Box-cutting entails digging a circular or squarish pit at least 5 sq. metre in width up to a depth of 400 feet.  Rat-hole mining is largely unregulated, and miners have to work without proper ventilation, safety gear, and any structural support.  The narrow and vertical nature of the pits makes them prone to collapse, leading to accidents and fatalities.  The National Green Tribunal (NGT) banned rat-hole mining in 2014 for being unscientific, although the practice remains widespread. Recently in news :  A one-member panel appointed by the High Court of Meghalaya to handle coal-related issues has flagged the lack of progress in restoring the environment damaged by rat-hole coal mining in the northeastern State.  The High Court appointed Justice Katakey in April 2022 to recommend measures to the Meghalaya government in compliance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court. Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium, New Delhi / मेजर ध्यानचंद नेशनल स्टेडियम, नई दिल्ली
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel Stadium, Gujarat / सरदार वल्लभभाई पटेल स्टेडियम, गुजरात

answer: Option B Explanation / व्याख्या: • The Reserve Bank of India launched three key surveys for November 2025: Inflation Expectations Survey of Households (IESH), Rural Consumer Confidence Survey (RCCS), and Urban Consumer Confidence Survey (UCCS). • भारतीय रिज़र्व बैंक ने नवंबर 2025 के लिए तीन प्रमुख सर्वेक्षण शुरू किए: इन्फ्लेशन एक्सपेक्टेशंस सर्वे ऑफ हाउसहोल्ड्स (IESH), रूरेल कंज्यूमर कॉन्फिडेंस सर्वे (RCCS) और अर्बन कंज्यूमर कॉन्फिडेंस सर्वे (UCCS)। • These surveys provide essential inputs for monetary policy formulation. • ये सर्वेक्षण मौद्रिक नीति निर्माण के लिए महत्वपूर्ण जानकारी प्रदान करते हैं। • IESH collects households’ perceptions on price movements and inflation across 19 major Indian cities. • IESH 19 प्रमुख भारतीय शहरों में कीमतों में उतार-चढ़ाव और मुद्रास्फीति पर परिवारों की धारणा एकत्र करता है। • RCCS is a bi-monthly survey capturing rural and semi-urban household views on economic situation, employment, prices, income and spending across 31 States/UTs. • RCCS एक द्विमासिक सर्वेक्षण है, जो 31 राज्यों/केंद्र शासित प्रदेशों में ग्रामीण और अर्ध-शहरी परिवारों की आर्थिक स्थिति, रोजगार, कीमतें, आय और खर्च पर राय एकत्र करता है। • UCCS is also bi-monthly and gathers urban consumer sentiments on economy, employment, income, spending and price trends across 19 cities. • UCCS भी द्विमासिक है और 19 शहरों में शहरी परिवारों से अर्थव्यवस्था, रोजगार, आय, खर्च और कीमतों के रुझान पर विचार एकत्र करता है। No. 1 PLATFORM FOR GOVT. question: Ques: When was the Mudh-Nyoma (Nyoma) Airbase in Ladakh operationalised?
answer: Option B Explanation / व्याख्या: • Mudh-Nyoma (Nyoma) Airbase in Ladakh was operationalised on 13 November 2025, with Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh landing in a C-130J Super Hercules aircraft. • लद्दाख में मुड-नयोमा (नयोमा) एयरबेस 13 नवंबर 2025 को परिचालन में आया, जिसमें एयर चीफ मार्शल ए.पी. सिंह ने C-130J सुपर हर्क्यूलिस विमान से उतराई की। • The base, located ~25 km from the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China at an altitude of ~13,700 ft, was developed at a cost of ~₹218 crore by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) and features a

Follow Us : Official Site Youtube WhatsApp Telegram Insta FB About Futures and options :  Futures and options are two fundamental types of derivatives in financial markets.  They are financial contracts that derive their value from the performance of an underlying asset, such as stocks, commodities, currencies, or indexes.  These instruments are used for hedging risks, speculating on price movements, and gaining leverage in financial markets.  A futures contract is a standardized agreement to buy or sell a specific quantity of an asset at a predetermined price on a specific future date.  An options contract gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call option) or sell (put option) an underlying asset at a specified price (strike price) before or on a specified date. question: Ques : What is the name of the new rules being notified to make Indian Standard Time (IST) mandatory across India?
explanation: • The Government of India is set to notify the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2025 to make the use of Indian Standard Time (IST) mandatory for legal, commercial, digital, and administrative purposes. • IST (UTC+5:30) is calculated from the 82°30’E meridian which passes through Mirzapur, Uttar Pradesh and is maintained by CSIR-NPL. • Historically, regions like Assam use an informal time called ‘Chaibagan Time’, which is one hour ahead of IST, introduced by British tea companies for productivity. • The move towards ‘One Nation, One Time’ seeks to eliminate multiple time practices and standardize official timing across the country. explanation: • The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has suggested new restrictions, including a Rs 1 crore minimum investment requirement for participants in securitization activities. • This effort, which targets both RBI-regulated originators and unregulated companies, aims to expedite investment processes while protecting investor interests. • The proposal also limited the number of investors in private placements, enabling only 200 investors to purchase securitized debt instruments (SDIs) produced privately. • If this limit is surpassed, the issuance must be classed as a public one. About securitized debt instruments : • SDIs are financial instruments formed by pooling several types of debt, such as loans, mortgages, or receivables, and then selling them as securities to investors. • This procedure, known as securitisation, allows the originator (often a bank) to turn illiquid assets into liquid ones, so offering an alternate source of funding. • Public SDI offers should be open for at least three days and no more than ten days. • Originators must maintain at least 10% risk exposure in the securitized pool (5% for receivables with a maturity of up to 24 months), aligning their interests with investors. question: Ques: Which companies signed a Memorandum to integrate drone technology into rural enterprises in India?

answer: Option D Explanation / व्याख्या: • AVPL International and CSC e-Governance Services India Limited signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to integrate drone technology into rural enterprises and empower rural entrepreneurs across India. • AVPL इंटरनेशनल और CSC ई-गवर्नेंस सर्विसेज इंडिया लिमिटेड ने ग्रामीण उद्यमों में ड्रोन तकनीक को शामिल करने और भारत भर में ग्रामीण उद्यमियों को सशक्त बनाने के लिए एक समझौता ज्ञापन (MoU) पर हस्ताक्षर किए। • The initiative aims to create jobs and new income opportunities for rural entrepreneurs through Drone-as-a-Service and precision agriculture techniques like spraying, crop monitoring, and yield optimization. • इस पहल का उद्देश्य ड्रोन-एज़-ए-सर्विस और सटीक कृषि तकनीकों जैसे छिड़काव, फसल निगरानी और उत्पादन अनुकूलन के माध्यम से ग्रामीण उद्यमियों के लिए रोजगार और नए आय अवसर पैदा करना है। • Under the MoU, AVPL International will provide its ‘Viraj Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS)’ agri drones, spare parts, and training programs via CSC’s network, which connects over 5 lakh Village Level Entrepreneurs. • MoU के तहत, AVPL इंटरनेशनल अपने ‘विराज अनमैन्ड एयरक्राफ्ट सिस्टम (UAS)’ कृषि ड्रोन, स्पेयर पार्ट्स और प्रशिक्षण कार्यक्रम CSC के नेटवर्क के माध्यम से प्रदान करेगी, जो 5 लाख से अधिक ग्राम स्तर के उद्यमियों से जुड़ा है। No. 1 PLATFORM FOR GOVT. question: Ques: What is the purpose of the “Startup Common Application Journey” launched on the Jan Samarth portal?
options: To provide subsidies for new startups / नए स्टार्टअप के लिए सब्सिडी प्रदान करना

To offer a unified digital platform for startups to access credit across all Indian PSBs / सभी भारतीय सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों में स्टार्टअप्स को ऋण उपलब्ध कराने हेतु एकीकृत डिजिटल प्लेटफ़ॉर्म प्रदान करना
To promote export-related services / निर्यात-संबंधी सेवाओं को बढ़ावा देना
To provide tax benefits for startups / स्टार्टअप्स को कर लाभ प्रदान करना
To support startup incubation centres / स्टार्टअप इनक्यूबेशन केंद्रों का समर्थन करना
answer: Option B Explanation / व्याख्या: • Department of Financial Services launched the “Startup Common Application Journey” on the Jan Samarth portal to provide a unified digital platform for startups to access credit across all Indian Public Sector Banks. • वित्तीय सेवाएं विभाग ने जन समर्थ पोर्टल पर “स्टार्टअप कॉमन एप्लिकेशन जर्नी” शुरू की, जिसका उद्देश्य सभी भारतीय सार्वजनिक क्षेत्र के बैंकों में स्टार्टअप्स को ऋण प्राप्त करने के लिए एकीकृत डिजिटल प्लेटफ़ॉर्म उपलब्ध कराना है। • The initiative, supported by a Model Loan Scheme, offers loans up to Rs 20 crore under the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups (CGSS) operated by the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company under DPIIT, Ministry of Commerce & Industry. • यह पहल मॉडल लोन योजना द्वारा समर्थित है और वाणिज्य एवं उद्योग मंत्रालय के अंतर्गत DPIIT के तहत संचालित नेशनल क्रेेडिट गारंटी ट्रस्टी कंपनी द्वारा स्टार्टअप्स के लिए क्रेेडिट गारंटी योजना (CGSS) के तहत 20 करोड़ रुपये तक का ऋण प्रदान करती है। • The Jan Samarth portal, launched in June 2022, serves as a single digital platform linking eligible beneficiaries to 14 credit-linked government schemes. • जून 2022 में शुरू किया गया जन समर्थ पोर्टल एक एकल डिजिटल प्लेटफ़ॉर्म है, जो पात्र लाभार्थियों को 14 क्रेेडिट- लिंक्ड सरकारी योजनाओं से जोड़ता है। No. 1 PLATFORM FOR GOVT. Unless instructed otherwise, assume that fractions, negatives, and zero are all included in the set of potential values. 3. By starting with the easier statement, you simplify the decision tree and leverage easier information first. 4. The Earth’s magnetic field plays a crucial role in sustaining life on the planet. Apart from aiding navigation, it acts as a protective shield that deflects high-energy radiation and charged particles emitted by the sun. Without this invisible barrier, solar radiation could severely damage the atmosphere and living organisms on Earth. For many years, geologists believed that when the Earth’s magnetic field reversed — meaning the north and south magnetic poles swapped places — the transition occurred relatively quickly, typically within about 10,000 years. However, a recent study published in Communications Earth & Environment has challenged this long-standing assumption. An international team of researchers from France, Japan, and the United States investigated the Earth’s magnetic history and discovered evidence suggesting that some magnetic reversals may take much longer than previously thought. Their findings indicate that certain reversals could extend over tens of thousands of years, leaving the planet with a weakened magnetic shield for extended periods. Scientists have identified hundreds of magnetic reversals throughout the Earth’s geological past. Yet most detailed data about these events comes from the last 17 million years, which represents only a small portion of the Earth’s approximately 4.5-billion-year history. Based on this relatively limited dataset, many scientists had concluded that the typical duration of a reversal was about 10,000 years, considering it an inherent characteristic of the Earth’s geodynamo. The geodynamo refers to the mechanism inside the planet in which the movement of molten iron in the outer core generates the magnetic field. To determine whether the previously accepted timeframe applied to earlier periods as well, the researchers analysed deep-sea sediment cores collected during an international drilling expedition in the North Atlantic Ocean. These sediments had accumulated on the ocean floor around 40 million years ago during the Eocene epoch. As layers of mud gradually formed, tiny magnetic minerals within the sediments aligned themselves with the Earth’s magnetic field at that time. Once buried under subsequent layers, these minerals preserved a permanent record of the direction and strength of the magnetic field. Using advanced techniques such as X-ray scanning and magnetic measurements, the scientists examined these sediment records to reconstruct past magnetic activity. They also used a method known as astronomical tuning, which aligns sediment layers with known cycles in the Earth’s orbital tilt, to determine the timing of these events more accurately. The results revealed that one magnetic reversal lasted about 18,000 years, while another extended for nearly 70,000 years. These durations are significantly longer than the 2,000 to 12,000 years typically observed in more recent geological records. The 70,000-year reversal was especially ENGLISH WITH NIMISHA BANSAL ​ ​ ​ ​ 15 complex, showing a precursor phase and several “rebounds” in which the magnetic field attempted to stabilise before fully reversing. Computer simulations of the Earth’s core further suggested that such prolonged reversals are a natural, though uncommon, feature of the geodynamo. During these long transitions, the magnetic field weakens considerably. As a result, the Earth’s atmosphere and surface life could be exposed to increased levels of solar radiation. Researchers believe that these extended periods of weak magnetic protection may have influenced ancient environments and possibly even affected the evolutionary history of life on Earth. Q1. Training a frontier AI model requires massive financial investment in computing infrastructure and carefully prepared datasets. However, a controversial method known as distillation allows competitors to reproduce advanced AI capabilities at much lower cost. Instead of developing a model independently, developers repeatedly query a powerful “teacher” model and use its responses to train a smaller “student” model. Over time, the student model learns to imitate the reasoning patterns of the teacher without bearing the original development expenses. Recently, the AI company Anthropic alleged that several Chinese laboratories conducted such extraction activities on a large scale by generating millions of queries to capture the capabilities of its Claude model. According to these claims, the extraction process depended on a large network of fraudulent accounts designed to obtain high-quality responses. AI companies generally try to prevent such practices through rate limits and blocking mechanisms. However, attackers can bypass these safeguards by using commercial proxy services, which allow internet traffic to appear as if it originates from multiple devices and locations. By spreading queries across numerous apparent users, attackers can avoid detection and continue collecting large volumes of training data. Many commercial proxy networks rely on compromised internet-connected devices. Investigations have found that numerous proxy IP addresses originate from hacked household equipment such as routers and smart appliances. Most device owners remain unaware that their internet connections are being used for large-scale data extraction. By rotating queries through these residential networks, automated activity can resemble normal human behaviour, thereby reducing the effectiveness of traditional security measures based on IP monitoring. The growing availability of proxy services has lowered the technical barriers to distillation attacks, enabling smaller or emerging companies to achieve advanced performance levels at reduced cost. This situation has encouraged what some analysts describe as a parasitic economy, in which certain firms benefit by exploiting existing AI innovations rather than developing original technologies. Such strategies may also help companies overcome restrictions on access to advanced computer chips by relying on established foreign models instead of building new ones from scratch. In response, AI companies are developing new detection techniques that focus on behavioural patterns rather than network sources. Instead of relying solely on suspicious IP addresses, researchers examine the statistical characteristics of incoming queries. Distillation attempts typically involve carefully organized ENGLISH WITH NIMISHA BANSAL ​ ​ ​ ​ 14 questions covering a wide range of topics in a systematic manner. These structured patterns differ significantly from the irregular and topic-focused queries usually generated by human users. Behaviour-based detection methods may reduce the effectiveness of proxy networks. Even if attackers disguise their locations, systematic query patterns may reveal attempts to train competing models. However, those attempting distillation may respond by adding random variations to their queries in order to resemble ordinary user behaviour. Consequently, the competition between AI developers and model imitators is evolving into a complex technological contest involving both advanced infrastructure and sophisticated analytical techniques. Early this year, the death of Craig, one of Africa’s rare “super tusker” elephants, in Amboseli National Park drew global tributes. Photographs of his enormous ivory tusks, almost touching the ground as he walked beneath Mount Kilimanjaro, resurfaced widely. Tourists, safari guides, and wildlife photographers remembered him as calm and regal. Over time, Craig had become more than an elephant — he symbolised wilderness, survival, tourism, and conservation. Elephants with such large tusks are now extremely rare. Decades of ivory poaching selectively removed big-tusked individuals, leaving behind animals with smaller ivory. Craig thus represented a vanishing genetic lineage. At the same time, he supported local livelihoods. Safaris, lodges, and nearby communities benefited from visitors who travelled long distances just to see him. Yet his story highlights an important truth: conservation does not operate at the level of individuals but at the level of populations, habitats, and ecosystems. Craig’s fame began with something simple — a name. Born into a well-studied herd observed by biologist Cynthia Moss, he grew up in public view. Naming wild animals transforms them from anonymous members of a species into characters in a story. People follow their lives, celebrate milestones, and mourn their deaths. Zoos and wildlife parks have long relied on such “star” animals to attract attention and funding. For instance, Pesto, a king penguin chick at Sea Life Aquarium Melbourne, became a viral sensation, significantly boosting visitor numbers. The practice of naming individuals became popular in the 1960s when primatologists Jane Goodall and Dian Fossey named chimpanzees and gorillas instead of numbering them. David Greybeard and Digit became memorable personalities, creating empathy and public engagement. However, conservation science has always remained focused on sustaining populations rather than saving particular animals. India has seen similar examples. Machli, the celebrated tigress of Ranthambore National Park, drew thousands of tourists and generated substantial revenue. Her presence supported conservation indirectly by sustaining tourism and local incomes. However, wildlife tourism centred on celebrity animals can exceed ecological limits. Resorts expand, safari vehicles crowd sightings, and attention narrows to charismatic species rather than entire ecosystems. Emotional attachment often blurs the line between caring for individuals and conserving species. In natural ecosystems, injury and death regulate populations. Saving a single animal rarely alters long-term trends unless the species is critically endangered. Experts like K. Ullas Karanth argue that resources are better ENGLISH WITH NIMISHA BANSAL ​ ​ ​ ​ 14 spent protecting habitats, maintaining genetic diversity, ensuring prey availability, and reducing human pressures. Yet individuals can matter in human-dominated landscapes. According to elephant researcher Ananda M. Kumar, certain animals can become ambassadors for coexistence, softening public attitudes and reducing conflict. Craig’s natural death reflects conservation success. He survived decades in a once-poaching-ravaged landscape. Celebrity animals capture attention and inspire emotion, but lasting conservation depends on habitat protection, law enforcement, scientific management, and community partnership. If Craig’s story leads to stronger anti-poaching efforts and protection of elephant corridors, his legacy will truly serve conservation.

Clearly, the mobility of people on such a large scale within cities, from their residential quarters to work areas, will be a test for urban planners. While policymakers have plans to construct smart cities, where the need for the mobility of workers will be substantially reduced, the fact remains that, unlike China, we do not see many of the newly emerging smart cities coming of age. In contrast, the metros/existing tier 1 cities are on an ever-expanding spree, leading to rising challenges for policymakers, such as meeting the transportation demand of workers. The government is increasingly focused on augmenting the public transport system to meet the urban mobility challenge. The 2025 Budget saw the launch of the PM e-Bus Sewa-Payment Security Mechanism, with the aim of improving urban bus transportation in India (nearly 10,000 urban buses). The PM Electric Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement (PM e-Drive) scheme was introduced, which will support the procurement of 14,000 new e-buses, 1,10,000 e-rickshaws, e-trucks, and e-ambulances. However, according to estimates, India needs 2,00,000 urban buses, but only 35,000 are operational (including e-buses). This is far below the requirement. Another initiative has been the greater emphasis on building metro networks and a higher allocation of funds in multiple metro/tier I cities to cater to the high density. This is in line with the trend seen in the recent Budget. However, as the Economic Survey that was released on the eve of the Budget on January 31, has cited, only 37% of urban residents in India have easy access to public transportation. In contrast, in Brazil and China, more than 50% of urban residents have convenient access to mass transit. Clearly, India is too far behind in developing an efficient public system. The development of a metro network is a long-term and costly venture. Much of it has been developed with the Centre’s funding. And invariably, most have yet to recover their total costs (which includes fixed and operational costs). In almost all metros, the ridership projected in the project document has still to be matched. So, recovering the cost may be a difficult proposition unless the route lies along a high-density route. Also, it has been observed that users are extremely fare sensitive, a fare rise invariably leads to a fall in footfalls. Invariably, consumers seek out their ways keeping in mind comfort, time and cost due to the high cost of last-mile connectivity from metro stations to their work/residence points. Unlike in some developed countries where public transport is highly subsidised in order to make metro transportation cheap, our government is not financially rich enough to dole out recurrent and large subsidies. India also needs cost-effective, road-based public transport for better last-mile connectivity. This year’s Budget has increased allocations for urban bus systems, thus continuing efforts to boost ENGLISH WITH NIMISHA BANSAL ​ ​ ​ ​ 38 capacity, especially in the metros. Yet, they often overlook trams and trolleybuses, which, based on a life cycle cost and revenue analysis, can outperform e-buses in financial terms and deserve serious policy consideration in India’s urban transport planning.

Relative speed is defined as the net speed of two entities when they are in motion. Other Options: ●​ Familiarise – Means make known; opposite of unexpected. ●​ Restrict – Means limit, which is contextually incorrect. ●​ Stabilise – Opposite of volatile; contradicts the sentence. ●​ Imitate – Means copy, unrelated to investor reaction. 2. More than one lakh gig and platform workers went on strike on December 31, demanding an immediate withdrawal of the 10–20 minute delivery model, which they argue compromises worker safety. In a memorandum submitted to Union Labour Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, worker unions highlighted unsafe working conditions, income insecurity, and lack of social protection. While the Union government views the four Labour Codes as a step toward social security for gig workers, the protest exposed deeper structural issues in India’s employment landscape. The debate around ultra-fast delivery models extends beyond consumer convenience. Critics argue that 10-minute delivery is not a genuine consumer necessity but a competitive strategy initiated by one company and quickly replicated by others. The marginal difference between a 10-minute and a 20–30 minute delivery may be negligible for consumers, but for delivery workers it significantly increases physical risk, stress, and income volatility. Speed, critics argue, is not generated by technology alone but extracted from human labour operating under unstable pay structures, algorithmic surveillance, and the constant threat of sudden account deactivation. Supporters of the model, however, point to its scale and economic contribution. Quick commerce has expanded rapidly, with the market expected to reach ₹1–1.5 lakh crore in the coming years, growing at nearly 28% annually. Online grocery alone is projected to grow by 40–50%. In a country where nearly 20 million people enter the workforce every year but only about two million jobs are created annually, gig platforms have filled a crucial employment gap, particularly for low-skilled workers. From this perspective, the key question becomes whether some form of employment is better than none at all. Regulation of the gig economy remains a contested issue. While India’s labour laws traditionally offer strong protection to full-time employees, gig work emerged outside this framework. Recent regulatory efforts acknowledge the need for worker protection but stop short of recognising gig workers as employees. Critics argue that platforms exercise significant control over pricing, task allocation, ratings, and penalties, making the “independent contractor” label misleading. If platforms control work, they should also bear legal obligations such as minimum income guarantees, accident insurance, and due process before deactivation. The Labour Codes, according to critics, are insufficient. They provide for welfare schemes like insurance and maternity benefits, but do not make them enforceable rights. Registration on portals such as e-SHRAM offers identification but little tangible security. Moreover, the Codes do not address algorithmic transparency, grievance redressal, or income stability.
